After leaving Aït Benhaddou, the road leads you toward Ouarzazate , a sun-drenched desert city often called “The Gateway to the Sahara.” Located about 30 kilometers from Aït Benhaddou, Ouarzazate sits at the intersection of the Draa, Dades, and Ziz valleys , making it a natural crossroads between Morocco’s mountains and its vast southern deserts.

Ouarzazate has a unique atmosphere — part cinematic, part traditional. It’s quieter than Marrakech, yet rich in history, architecture, and film culture. For many travelers, this is the ideal place to rest, refuel, and explore before continuing deeper into the desert.
Why Ouarzazate is Called “Hollywood of Africa”

Ouarzazate’s stunning landscapes and clear light have attracted filmmakers from around the world for decades. You’ll quickly notice how familiar the surroundings feel — countless Hollywood productions have been filmed here, turning this desert city into an open-air movie set.
Famous films and series shot in Ouarzazate and nearby Aït Benhaddou include
Lawrence of Arabia
Gladiator
Kingdom of Heaven
The Mummy
Game of Thrones

The Atlas Film Studios , one of the largest in the world, is a must-visit attraction. Visitors can tour enormous sets, including replicas of Egyptian temples, biblical palaces, and ancient cities — all standing in the middle of the desert.
Cultural and Historical Highlights
Beyond its cinematic fame, Ouarzazate offers a glimpse into Morocco’s southern heritage.

Taourirt Kasbah: Once the residence of the powerful Glaoui family, this labyrinthine fortress dominates the city’s center. Wander through its maze of corridors and admire the beautifully decorated rooms filled with traditional motifs and desert charm.
Musee du Cinema: Located near the kasbah, this small museum showcases movie props, costumes, and behind-the-scenes stories from decades of filmmaking.

Fint Oasis: Just 15 kilometers outside the city, this hidden green valley of palms and small Berber villages provides a refreshing contrast to the dry surroundings. It’s an excellent short detour for photography or a local meal with a view.
Where to Stay
Ouarzazate has a wide range of accommodation, from budget guesthouses to luxury kasbah-style hotels.
Recommended options
Le Berbere Palace: A five-star hotel famous for hosting film crews and offering top-tier comfort.
Dar Kamar: Boutique guesthouse set inside a restored kasbah, blending tradition and modernity.
Hotel La Perle du Sud: Affordable, with a pool and central location — great for short stays.
Spending one night in Ouarzazate allows you to explore its landmarks and enjoy a comfortable rest before the next part of your road trip.
Optional Detour: Skoura Oasis

If you have time, take a short drive east to Skoura , about 40 kilometers away. This fertile palm grove, known as the “Valley of a Thousand Kasbahs,” is dotted with traditional mud-brick fortresses and charming guesthouses. One of the highlights is Kasbah Amridil , featured on Morocco’s 50-dirham banknote — a beautiful example of desert architecture still inhabited by locals today.
Travel Tips
Ouarzazate has good facilities for travelers: ATMs, supermarkets, and petrol stations.
It’s a great place to buy desert essentials — scarves, sunglasses, and light clothing.
Roads from here become straighter and more open as you approach the Dades Valley, making driving easier.

5. Skoura to Dades Valley: The Road of a Thousand Kasbahs

Leaving Ouarzazate behind, the journey toward the Dades Valley is one of Morocco’s most visually stunning stretches. This section of your Marrakech to Merzouga road trip is often called “The Road of a Thousand Kasbahs” — a poetic name that perfectly captures the essence of the region. Here, lush palm groves, traditional mud-brick fortresses, and winding river valleys create a landscape that feels timeless and cinematic.
Distance and Driving Time
Distance: Around 120 kilometers (75 miles)
Driving Time: 2 to 3 hours, depending on stops

This leg of the journey takes you east through Skoura Oasis , then along the Valley of Roses , before reaching the dramatic Dades Gorges . The road is well-maintained, offering smooth driving and plenty of opportunities to stop for photos or to explore local villages.
Skoura Oasis: A Green Gem in the Desert

Skoura is a lush, fertile valley filled with palm groves, olive trees, and pomegranate orchards — a peaceful contrast to the dry mountains that surround it. It’s one of the few oases still inhabited and farmed traditionally.
What to see in Skoura
Kasbah Amridil: The most famous kasbah in the oasis, dating back to the 17th century. Its towers, courtyards, and preserved architecture offer a real glimpse of desert life centuries ago.
Palm Grove Walks: Take a short walk or bike ride among the palms, where locals still use ancient irrigation channels called khettaras .
Local Guesthouses: If you stayed overnight here, enjoy the tranquility — the sunrise light filtering through the palms is magical.
The Valley of Roses

Continuing east, the road follows the M’Goun River through the Valley of Roses , named after the Damask roses cultivated here for centuries. Every May, the nearby town of Kelaat M’Gouna hosts the famous Festival of Roses , celebrating the harvest with music, dancing, and markets selling rose water, perfumes, and oils.
Even outside the festival, this region is worth exploring — the terraced fields, clay villages, and pink hues of the mountains create an unforgettable landscape.
The Dades Valley and Gorges

After Kelaat M’Gouna, the road climbs gradually into the Dades Valley , where the scenery becomes increasingly dramatic. This area is often described as “Morocco’s Grand Canyon” — a series of red and orange cliffs carved by the Dades River over millennia.
Highlights
Boumalne Dades: The main town at the entrance of the gorges. It’s a good base for accommodation and local excursions.
The Monkey Fingers Rock Formation: Strange, finger-like cliffs that seem to grow out of the earth — a great photo stop.

The Dades Gorge Road (Tizi n’Boulmane): A winding mountain road famous for its zigzag turns and breathtaking viewpoints. Drive carefully, and stop at the Hotel Café Timzzillite panoramic terrace for one of the best views in southern Morocco.
Where to Stay
Spend one night in the Dades Valley to soak up the scenery and hospitality. Many family-run riads and guesthouses overlook the valley or are nestled within the gorge itself.
Recommended stays
Auberge Chez Pierre: Known for stunning views and excellent cuisine.
Riad Dades Paradise: A cozy stay with terraces overlooking the river.
Kasbah Tizzarouine: Offers traditional architecture and modern comfort.
Travel Tips
The roads in this area are narrow but generally well-paved. Drive slowly through villages and watch for livestock crossing.
Evenings can get cool, so bring a light jacket.
Make sure your camera or phone is fully charged — this section offers some of the most photogenic landscapes of the entire trip.
6. Todra Gorge: Nature’s Masterpiece

After exploring the Dades Valley, your journey continues toward the Todra Gorge , one of Morocco’s most dramatic natural wonders. This section of the Marrakech to Merzouga road trip offers a mix of adventure, stunning scenery, and insight into traditional Berber mountain life.
Distance and Driving Time
From Dades Valley to Todra Gorge: Approximately 80 kilometers (50 miles)
Driving Time: Around 2 hours

The route between Dades and Todra winds through arid hills and small villages before reaching Tinghir (or Tinerhir) — the gateway to the Todra Gorge. From Tinghir, it’s a short drive into the gorge itself, where the scenery suddenly becomes jaw-dropping.
The Road to Todra Gorge

The approach to Todra is spectacular. You’ll pass through lush palm groves and ancient mud-brick villages clinging to the hillside, all framed by the High Atlas Mountains . As you drive deeper, the canyon walls rise higher and higher — eventually towering up to 300 meters (984 feet) on either side.
The final stretch of road follows the Todra River , which continues to carve its way through the rock, leaving behind a narrow passage where sunlight barely reaches the ground in some spots.
What to See and Do

1. Explore the Gorge on Foot: Park your car and take a walk through the narrowest section of the canyon. The towering limestone walls, glowing in shades of orange and gold, make this one of Morocco’s most photographed spots. Early morning or late afternoon light creates a magical atmosphere for photos.

2. Rock Climbing: Todra Gorge is world-famous among rock climbers. With more than 150 climbing routes , it attracts adventurers from across the globe. Even if you’re not climbing, watching professionals scale the cliffs is an impressive sight.

3. Visit Tinghir Oasis: Before or after your visit, explore the Tinghir Palm Grove — a beautiful stretch of greenery filled with date palms, olive trees, and small farms. Walking paths lead through the oasis and traditional Berber villages, offering a glimpse of local life.
4. Local Handicrafts: The nearby villages sell handmade carpets, fossils, and pottery. Bargaining is expected, but always done with a smile.
Where to Eat and Stay
You’ll find small cafés and restaurants near the entrance to the gorge, many serving tagines, couscous, and fresh orange juice with mountain views.
Recommended stays near Todra Gorge
Auberge Le Festival Todra Gorge: Eco-lodge built into the rock itself, offering cave-style rooms and unbeatable views.
Hotel Kasbah Taborihte: Traditional Moroccan architecture and a pool overlooking the valley.
Maison d’Hôte Panorama Todra: A welcoming guesthouse with terrace views over the gorge.
Travel Tips
Best time to visit: Early morning or late afternoon for ideal lighting and cooler temperatures.
Footwear: Comfortable shoes are essential for walking on rocky terrain.
Photography tip: The contrast between shadow and sunlight in the gorge can be intense — use HDR or manual settings for best results.
Local Etiquette: Many families still live nearby. Always ask before photographing people or homes.
Why It’s a Must-See Stop

The Todra Gorge combines raw natural beauty with authentic Moroccan culture . Whether you’re hiking, taking photos, or simply sitting beside the river listening to the wind through the cliffs, it’s a place that captures the soul of the desert mountains.
7. Erfoud and Rissani: Gateway to the Sahara

After leaving Todra Gorge, the road opens up to the vast plains leading toward the Sahara Desert . This stage of the Marrakech to Merzouga road trip takes you through the towns of Erfoud and Rissani , small but culturally rich stops that serve as gateways to the golden dunes of Erg Chebbi .
Distance and Driving Time
From Todra Gorge to Erfoud: Approximately 150 kilometers (93 miles)
Driving Time: Around 2.5 to 3 hours

The journey transitions from mountain scenery to desert landscapes — rocky plateaus gradually give way to sandy expanses, palm groves, and sparse vegetation. It’s a visually dramatic shift, preparing travelers for the Sahara’s unique beauty.
Erfoud: Fossils and Dates
Known as the “fossil capital” of Morocco, Erfoud is a small town with a rich history and practical amenities for travelers.
Highlights
Fossil Workshops: Erfoud sits on ancient seabeds, and local artisans craft stunning fossil jewelry, decorative panels, and educational pieces. Perfect for souvenirs or photography.
Date Markets: The town produces some of Morocco’s finest dates. Sample deglet nour dates or enjoy date-based sweets and pastries.
Accommodation: Erfoud has a variety of hotels and desert lodges, ideal for an overnight stop before reaching Merzouga.
Rissani: Authentic Desert Life

Just a short drive from Erfoud, Rissani offers a more traditional Moroccan experience. Known as the historic caravan town that once linked Marrakech with the Sahara, Rissani is vibrant and full of life.
Things to do
Rissani Souk: A bustling traditional market where you can buy spices, carpets, and Berber handicrafts. The atmosphere is lively, with local merchants calling out to shoppers.
Historic Sites: Explore the old ksar (fortified village) ruins and mausoleums of local saints.
Try Local Cuisine: Sample Madfouna , a Berber-style baked bread stuffed with meat and vegetables, cooked in a traditional clay oven.
Rissani gives travelers a sense of authentic desert culture that larger tourist hubs sometimes lack, making it a worthwhile stop before venturing into Merzouga.
Preparing for Merzouga
After Rissani, the final stretch to Merzouga is short — about 35 kilometers (22 miles) — but you’ll begin to notice the desert landscape dominating the horizon.
Travel tips for this leg
Fill up on fuel and water in Erfoud or Rissani — services become scarce once you enter the dunes.
Carry snacks, sunscreen, and a hat for the desert heat.
Plan your arrival in Merzouga to coincide with either sunset or sunrise for the most magical dune experience.
Why Erfoud and Rissani Are Important Stops

These towns serve not just as practical waypoints but as cultural transitions . Erfoud introduces you to the natural history of the desert, while Rissani immerses you in the living traditions and commerce of desert communities. Stopping here ensures you arrive in Merzouga ready to fully appreciate the Sahara.
8. Merzouga and the Erg Chebbi Dunes

Finally, you reach Merzouga , the ultimate destination of this Marrakech to Merzouga road trip. Nestled at the edge of the Sahara Desert , Merzouga is a small village that opens onto the vast Erg Chebbi dunes , Morocco’s most famous sand sea. This is where the adventure truly comes alive — endless golden dunes, dramatic sunsets, and nights under a sky filled with stars.
Arrival and First Impressions

As you approach Merzouga, the flat desert landscape gradually gives way to rolling dunes that rise majestically from the earth. The colors shift throughout the day — from pale yellow in the morning to deep orange at sunset. It’s a photographer’s paradise and a sensory experience unlike anywhere else in Morocco.
Activities in Merzouga
Merzouga offers a variety of ways to experience the desert

1. Camel Trekking: The most iconic desert activity. Travel on the back of a camel through the dunes, ideally during sunset or sunrise , for breathtaking views. Many tours include an overnight stay in a desert camp.

2. Overnight Desert Camp: Experience traditional Berber hospitality in a luxury or semi-traditional desert camp . Stay in tents equipped with comfortable bedding, enjoy local meals, and gather around a campfire beneath the stars.

3. Sandboarding and 44 Adventures: For thrill-seekers, sliding down the dunes on a sandboard or exploring the desert in a 44 is exhilarating. Local guides provide equipment and ensure safety while showing hidden desert gems.
4. Stargazing: Far from city lights, Merzouga’s night sky is extraordinary. The Milky Way, shooting stars, and constellations are visible in astonishing clarity — a magical desert experience.
Local Culture and Villages

Merzouga is also home to Berber communities who have lived in harmony with the desert for centuries. Visitors can explore small villages, interact with locals, and learn about traditional crafts, music, and desert survival skills.
Tips
Respect local customs, especially when visiting private homes or villages.
Bargaining is common in the market, but always with respect and a smile.
Photography is welcome, but ask permission when capturing people’s portraits.
Where to Stay
Merzouga has accommodations ranging from luxury desert camps to budget guesthouses .
Recommended options
Luxury Desert Camp: Spacious tents with private bathrooms, traditional cuisine, and camel rides included.
Auberge Chez Pierre: A cozy guesthouse at the base of the dunes with excellent local meals.
Nomad Palace: Offers authentic Berber-style accommodations and dune excursions.
Staying at least one night in Merzouga is essential — it allows you to witness both sunrise and sunset over the dunes , which are completely different but equally spectacular.
Travel Tips
Best time to visit: Early morning for sunrise, late afternoon for sunset, and clear nights for stargazing.
Clothing: Lightweight layers, a scarf for sand, hat, sunglasses, and sunscreen. Nights can be chilly, so bring a warm layer.
Hydration: Carry water, especially during treks or dune climbs.
Guides: Hiring a local guide enhances safety and enriches the experience with cultural insights.
Why Merzouga is the Highlight

Merzouga and the Erg Chebbi dunes are the culmination of your road trip — a place where natural beauty, adventure, and local culture converge. From camel rides to starlit nights, the desert offers moments of quiet reflection and unforgettable memories. It’s the ultimate reward after days of exploring mountains, valleys, and oases on the road from Marrakech.
9. Optional Return Routes

After experiencing the magic of Merzouga, travelers face a choice: retrace their steps back to Marrakech or continue exploring Morocco along alternative routes. This section of the Marrakech to Merzouga road trip outlines options for returning or extending your journey, helping you plan a memorable conclusion.
Option 1: Return via the Same Route
The simplest choice is to drive back the same way you came, allowing for additional stops or more relaxed pacing.
Highlights along the return
Todra Gorge and Dades Valley: Catch sites you may have missed or revisit for different lighting and photography opportunities.
Ouarzazate and Aït Benhaddou: Spend another night at a kasbah or explore small villages along the way.
High Atlas Mountains: Enjoy the mountain scenery once more, especially if driving during sunrise or sunset.
Advantages
Familiar roads reduce navigation stress.
Opportunity to stop at favorite locations again.
Allows travelers to maintain a more structured schedule.
Option 2: Return via Fez (Circular Route)
For a longer, more adventurous route, you can head north from Merzouga toward Fez , passing through Errachidia, Ifrane, and Midelt .
Highlights along this route
Ifrane: Often called “Little Switzerland,” known for its alpine-style architecture and clean streets.
Middle Atlas Mountains: Scenic forests, lakes, and traditional Berber villages.
Azrou: Famous for its cedar forests and Barbary macaques.
Fez: Morocco’s cultural and spiritual capital, with a medina considered one of the world’s largest and most authentic.
Advantages
Creates a circular route that covers a different part of Morocco.
Introduces a new mix of landscapes: desert, mountains, and forests.
Provides opportunities for cultural immersion in Fez’s medina and crafts markets.
Option 3: Continue to the Sahara’s Southern Regions
Some travelers prefer to extend their desert adventure by heading south toward Zagora , M’Hamid , or even crossing into Mauritania for extended desert exploration.
Highlights
Vast empty desert landscapes with fewer tourists.
Authentic Berber villages and nomadic culture.
Opportunities for multi-day camel treks or desert camping under more remote conditions.
Advantages
Avoid retracing the same route.
Deepen your Sahara experience.
Ideal for adventurous travelers seeking solitude and extreme landscapes.
Travel Tips for the Return
Fuel and Supplies: Always refuel before leaving Merzouga; long stretches of road have few petrol stations.
Road Conditions: Roads toward Fez are generally good but can be mountainous and winding.
Time Management: Plan driving hours to avoid night driving in remote areas, particularly if self-driving.
Accommodation: Book ahead, especially in Fez or Ifrane, during peak tourist seasons.
Why Considering Return Routes Matters

The journey back can be as rewarding as the trip out. Choosing the right return route allows travelers to explore different landscapes, historical towns, and cultural highlights , extending the adventure while ensuring a safe and enjoyable experience.
10. Practical Tips for the Marrakech to Merzouga Road Trip

A successful road trip across Morocco requires preparation, local knowledge, and a few insider tips. This section provides practical advice to help travelers navigate the journey safely, comfortably, and enjoyably.
1. Driving Tips
Road Conditions: Most main roads are paved and well-maintained, but expect narrow mountain passes, sharp turns, and occasional potholes . Drive cautiously, especially in the High Atlas Mountains.
Traffic: In rural areas, watch for donkeys, livestock, and slow-moving trucks . In towns, expect pedestrians and chaotic intersections.
Speed Limits: Stick to posted limits — generally 60–80 km/h in towns and 100–120 km/h on highways .
2. Navigation
Offline Maps: Download offline maps from Google Maps or Maps.me , as mobile coverage may be limited in mountains and desert regions.
GPS Devices: Useful if your smartphone battery is low, but always carry a paper map as a backup.
Local Advice: Don’t hesitate to ask locals for directions — Moroccan drivers are often very helpful.
3. Safety
Travel During Daylight: Avoid night driving in remote areas, as street lighting is minimal and road conditions can be challenging.
Emergency Numbers: Morocco’s general emergency number is 19 , and roadside assistance may take time in remote areas.
Health Precautions: Carry a basic first-aid kit and enough water, especially when crossing the desert.
4. Money and Payments
Cash: Many small towns and desert villages do not accept cards. Carry sufficient Moroccan dirhams for fuel, meals, and souvenirs.
ATMs: Available in major towns like Marrakech, Ouarzazate, Erfoud, and Rissani. Fill up before heading into the desert.
Tipping: Expected in restaurants, hotels, and for guides. 10–15% is standard.
5. Accommodation Tips
Booking: During peak season (spring and autumn), book ahead for Merzouga and mountain regions.
Riads and Kasbahs: Offers authentic Moroccan experiences with traditional décor.
Desert Camps: Check reviews for comfort, food quality, and camel trek inclusions.
6. Packing Essentials
Lightweight clothing for daytime heat and warm layers for cool nights.
Sunglasses, hat, and sunscreen to protect from the strong desert sun.
Comfortable walking shoes for mountain passes and desert dunes.
Reusable water bottle and snacks for long stretches between towns.
Camera, power bank, and spare batteries — the scenery is stunning at every stop.
7. Cultural Etiquette
Dress Respectfully: Morocco is a Muslim-majority country; modest clothing is appreciated in villages and rural areas.
Photography: Always ask permission before photographing people, particularly women.
Greetings: A simple “Salam Alaikum” (peace be upon you) is appreciated and opens doors to friendly interactions.
8. Fuel and Food Stops
Refuel frequently — gas stations are sparse in the desert.
Try local cuisine at small roadside cafés: tagines, couscous, and fresh fruit juice.
Carry water and snacks for long drives between villages and oases.
Conclusion: Wrapping Up the Marrakech to Merzouga Road Trip

The journey from Marrakech to Merzouga is more than just a road trip; it is an unforgettable adventure that immerses travelers in Morocco’s diverse landscapes, rich culture, and timeless traditions . From the vibrant medina of Marrakech to the towering golden dunes of Erg Chebbi, this route offers a perfect blend of history, natural beauty, and authentic experiences . Along the way, travelers encounter the breathtaking High Atlas Mountains with their winding passes and Berber villages, explore the historic kasbahs of Aït Benhaddou and the cinematic landscapes of Ouarzazate, and discover the dramatic gorges and lush palm oases of the Dades Valley and Todra Gorge. Cultural gems like Erfoud and Rissani provide a glimpse into desert life, with bustling souks, traditional crafts, and fossil workshops, before culminating in the ultimate desert experience of Merzouga — where camel treks, starlit nights, and panoramic sand dunes create memories that last a lifetime. This road trip stands out for its diverse scenery, cultural immersion, and perfect balance of adventure and relaxation , offering countless photographic opportunities and moments of reflection. To make the most of this journey, travelers should plan at least 4–7 days, stay flexible to embrace spontaneous stops, respect local customs, and remain prepared for desert conditions. Driving from Marrakech to Merzouga is a journey where history, culture, and nature converge, leaving every traveler with experiences and memories that will stay with them forever.

title: The Ultimate Backpacker’s Guide to Morocco on a Budget
seoTitle: The Ultimate Morocco Backpacking Guide: Unforgettable Adventures on a Budget
description: Explore Morocco on a budget with this Morocco backpacking guide. Discover affordable accommodation, cheap eats, budget-friendly activities, and insider tips for Marrakech, Fes, Chefchaouen, the Sahara Desert, and more.

blocks.x: Morocco is one of the most captivating destinations for backpackers, offering a rich mix of culture, history, and natural beauty—all without breaking the bank. This Morocco backpacking guide is designed specifically for travelers exploring the country on a budget, providing practical tips, insider advice, and cost-saving strategies. From wandering the bustling medinas of Marrakech and Fes to trekking the Atlas Mountains or camping under the Sahara stars, this guide will help you experience Morocco’s magic affordably. Whether you’re seeking adventure, cultural immersion, or unforgettable culinary experiences, this Morocco backpacking guide ensures you make the most of your journey without overspending.
Planning Your Budget Trip

Planning is the key to a successful and affordable Moroccan adventure. With the right timing, budget strategies, and essential travel info, you can enjoy Morocco without overspending. Here’s how to get started:
1. Best Time to Visit Morocco

Spring (March–May) and Autumn (September–November) offer mild temperatures and fewer crowds, ideal for budget travelers. Summer can be very hot, especially in the desert and southern cities, which may increase costs for air-conditioned stays. Winter is cheaper in many cities but can be cold in the Atlas Mountains. Traveling off-peak can save on flights, accommodation, and tours.
2. Visa and Travel Requirements

Most European, North American, and some Asian travelers do not require a visa for stays up to 90 days. Make sure your passport is valid for at least six months. Travel insurance is highly recommended and affordable through many providers—this can save huge costs if something goes wrong.
3. Budgeting Tips

Average daily costs: Budget accommodation: $10–$25 per night, Meals: $5–$15 per day if eating street food or local cafés, Transport: $5–$20 per day using public transport. Eat at local markets rather than tourist restaurants, take public transport instead of taxis, and stay in hostels, riads, or guesthouses with shared rooms. Haggle politely in souks and research prices before buying tours or souvenirs.
With careful planning, this Morocco backpacking guide will help you explore the country affordably and efficiently.
Affordable Accommodation Options
Finding budget-friendly accommodation in Morocco is easy if you know where to look. From hostels to riads and guesthouses, there are plenty of options that offer comfort without draining your wallet.
1. Hostels and Riads

Hostels are ideal for solo backpackers or groups, offering dorm-style rooms and opportunities to meet other travelers. Prices typically range from $8–$20 per night. Budget riads—traditional Moroccan houses converted into guesthouses—provide a more authentic experience. Some offer shared rooms or small private rooms at $15–$30 per night. Booking in advance can help you secure the best deals, especially in Marrakech, Fes, and Chefchaouen.
2. Guesthouses and Couchsurfing

Guesthouses offer a local experience at low cost, usually including breakfast. Couchsurfing is a free alternative, allowing you to stay with locals and gain insider knowledge of the city. Always check reviews and communicate clearly with hosts to ensure safety and comfort.
3. Camping and Desert Stays

For adventurous backpackers, camping in the Atlas Mountains or the Sahara Desert is a memorable and affordable option. Shared desert camps can cost $15–$40 per night and often include dinner and entertainment. Bring basic camping gear if you prefer independent camping in natural areas.

By choosing hostels, riads, guesthouses, or camping, backpackers can enjoy Morocco comfortably while sticking to a tight budget. This Morocco backpacking guide highlights the best low-cost lodging options across the country.
Getting Around on a Budget
Transportation is a major part of any travel budget, but Morocco offers many affordable ways to get from city to city and explore its towns and landscapes without overspending.
1. Public Transport

Buses and trains are the most cost-effective ways to travel between cities. The national train network, ONCF , connects major cities like Casablanca, Marrakech, Fes, and Rabat. Ticket prices are reasonable, and booking in advance can save money. Local buses and shared taxis (known as grand taxis ) are great for shorter distances and cost $1–$5 depending on distance.
2. Car Rentals and Hitchhiking

Car rentals are an option for those who want flexibility, especially when exploring rural areas or the desert. Renting a small car can cost $20–$35 per day, but fuel prices are relatively low. Hitchhiking is possible in Morocco and is generally safe during the day, but always use caution and avoid remote areas at night.
3. Walking and Cycling

Walking is the best way to explore medinas, markets, and historic neighborhoods. Many cities have pedestrian-friendly streets where public transport isn’t necessary. Bike rentals are available in cities like Marrakech and Essaouira for around $5–$10 per day, allowing for cheap and flexible local travel.

Using a combination of public transport, walking, cycling, and selective car rentals or hitchhiking, backpackers can navigate Morocco affordably and efficiently. Following these tips, this Morocco backpacking guide ensures you save money while seeing more of the country.
Affordable Food and Drink
Eating well in Morocco doesn’t have to be expensive. From street food stalls to local cafés, there are countless ways to enjoy delicious Moroccan cuisine on a budget.
1. Street Food and Markets

Street food is not only cheap but also an authentic way to taste Morocco. Must-try budget-friendly dishes include b’ssara (fava bean soup), sfenj (Moroccan doughnuts), briouats (savory pastries), and tagine served at small local stalls. Markets (souks) are also great for fresh fruit, nuts, and snacks. Prices typically range from $1–$5 per item.
2. Local Cafés and Bakeries

Local cafés offer affordable meals, mint tea, and Moroccan pastries. A simple lunch of sandwiches or couscous can cost $2–$5. Bakeries often sell bread and sweet treats at very low prices, making them ideal for a quick snack or breakfast.
3. Self-Catering Tips

Shopping at local markets and preparing your own meals is another great way to save. Many hostels and riads provide kitchen facilities where you can cook simple dishes. Buying fresh vegetables, bread, eggs, and cheese can keep daily food costs under $5–$10 while giving you more control over your meals.

By combining street food, local cafés, and self-catering, backpackers can enjoy Morocco’s culinary delights without overspending. This section of the Morocco backpacking guide ensures you eat well while sticking to a budget.
Budget-Friendly Activities
Morocco is full of experiences that don’t have to cost a fortune. From exploring historic cities to trekking in nature, backpackers can enjoy plenty of low-cost adventures.
1. Cultural Experiences

Many museums, mosques, and historic sites have low entry fees or are free to visit. Explore the medinas of Fes and Marrakech, walk through vibrant souks, and admire the architecture of palaces and riads. Participating in local festivals or cultural events is another affordable way to experience Moroccan traditions.
2. Nature and Adventure

Hiking in the Atlas Mountains, wandering through valleys, or exploring waterfalls are mostly free and provide incredible views. For the Sahara Desert, shared desert treks and camping can be affordable ($15–$40), offering an unforgettable adventure on a budget.
3. City Exploration

Walking tours are often free or donation-based, allowing you to explore cities like Marrakech, Casablanca, and Chefchaouen at your own pace. Markets, gardens, and public squares are perfect for soaking in the local atmosphere without spending much.

By focusing on cultural sites, natural landscapes, and self-guided city exploration, backpackers can have rich experiences while keeping expenses low. This Morocco backpacking guide highlights activities that are both memorable and budget-friendly.
Start Your Moroccan Adventure Today!

Ready to explore Morocco on a budget? Grab this Morocco backpacking guide and plan your trip with confidence. Discover affordable accommodation, cheap eats, cultural experiences, and unforgettable adventures—all while sticking to your budget. Don’t wait—your Moroccan journey awaits!
Plan Your Budget Trip Now
Click Here
Safety and Health on a Budget
Traveling safely and staying healthy is essential, even when backpacking on a budget. Morocco is generally safe for tourists, but being prepared helps you avoid unexpected costs.
1. Staying Safe
Stick to well-populated areas, especially at night.
Keep your valuables secure; use a money belt or lockable backpack.
Be cautious with strangers offering unsolicited help or tours.
When visiting crowded markets, be mindful of pickpockets.
2. Affordable Healthcare
Pharmacies in Morocco are widely available and offer low-cost medications for common ailments.
Public hospitals provide basic healthcare at affordable rates. Travel insurance is still recommended to cover emergencies.
3. Travel Vaccinations and Precautions
Standard vaccinations such as tetanus, hepatitis A, and typhoid are recommended.
Drinking bottled or filtered water and eating freshly cooked food reduces the risk of foodborne illness.
Carry a small first aid kit to avoid buying expensive items while traveling.

By taking simple precautions, backpackers can explore Morocco safely and avoid unnecessary expenses. Following these tips, this Morocco backpacking guide ensures your trip remains enjoyable and worry-free.
Money-Saving Hacks
Stretching your budget in Morocco is easier than you think if you know a few insider tips. These hacks help you enjoy more while spending less.
1. Bargaining and Haggling

Haggling is expected in markets and souks. Start by offering half the asking price and negotiate politely. Be confident but friendly—it’s part of the local shopping culture. Avoid touristy shops where prices are fixed. For a complete guide to shopping smart and bargaining like a local, check out our Guide to Moroccan Souks: What to Buy and How to Bargain
2. Using Apps and Online Deals

Use booking apps to find discounted hostels, riads, and tours. Transportation apps and websites can reveal cheaper bus or train tickets if booked early. Food apps or review sites can point you to local budget-friendly eateries.
3. Avoiding Hidden Fees

Always check if hostel or riad prices include taxes or service fees. When taking taxis, insist on the meter or agree on a price beforehand. Bring cash in local currency to avoid ATM or exchange rate fees.
4. Combining Activities for Savings
Walking tours, free museums, and self-guided excursions are a great way to see more for less. Group tours often cost less per person than private tours.

By applying these money-saving strategies, backpackers can make the most of their Moroccan adventure without overspending. This Morocco backpacking guide equips you with the tools to travel smarter and save more.
Sample Itineraries for Budget Travelers
Planning a trip can be overwhelming, so these sample itineraries show how to explore Morocco on a budget, whether you have a week, two weeks, or want a desert-focused adventure.
1. 7-Day Morocco on a Budget
Day 1–2: Marrakech – Explore the medina, Jemaa el-Fnaa square, and souks. Stay in a budget riad or hostel.
Day 3–4: Atlas Mountains – Take a shared taxi or bus to Imlil, hike trails, and stay in a local guesthouse.
Day 5: Essaouira – Bus to the coastal town for fresh seafood, beaches, and relaxed atmosphere.
Day 6–7: Marrakech – Return to Marrakech for any last sightseeing and shopping before departure.
2. 2-Week Backpacking Adventure
Days 1–3: Fes – Wander the medina, visit tanneries, and enjoy local street food.
Days 4–5: Chefchaouen – Explore the blue city, hike nearby trails, and stay in budget riads.
Days 6–8: Marrakech & Atlas Mountains – Combine city exploration with mountain treks.
Days 9–11: Sahara Desert – Travel to Merzouga for affordable desert camping experiences.
Days 12–14: Casablanca & Rabat – Visit Hassan II Mosque, medinas, and relax in coastal towns before flying home.
Desert-Focused Budget Trip
Day 1–2: Marrakech – Arrive in Morocco and explore the vibrant city of Marrakech. Wander through the medina, visit Jemaa el-Fnaa square, and soak in the local culture.
Day 3: Drive/Bus to Merzouga – Travel to Merzouga using shared transport for an economical route. This small desert town is your gateway to the Sahara.

Day 4–5: Sahara Desert Camping – Experience unforgettable adventures with camel rides, star-gazing, and traditional Berber meals in the desert. For a detailed guide on planning your desert trip, including budget tips and optional tours, check out our How to Plan the Perfect Sahara Desert Trip
Day 6: Return to Marrakech – Travel back to Marrakech, stopping at small towns along the way to experience more of Morocco’s culture and landscapes.

These itineraries show how to combine adventure, culture, and relaxation while staying within a backpacker’s budget. Using this Morocco backpacking guide , travelers can plan their trips efficiently and affordably.
Conclusion: Your Essential Morocco Backpacking Guide

Morocco is a dream destination for backpackers, offering a unique mix of culture, history, and natural beauty without breaking the bank. With careful planning, smart budgeting, and the tips provided in this Morocco backpacking guide , travelers can explore bustling medinas, hike the Atlas Mountains, experience the Sahara Desert, and savor local cuisine—all while staying on a budget. By choosing affordable accommodation, using public transport, enjoying street food, and taking advantage of free or low-cost activities, backpackers can make the most of their Moroccan adventure. This guide proves that traveling in Morocco doesn’t require a big budget—only a sense of adventure, curiosity, and a willingness to immerse yourself in the country’s rich culture.

title: What City Matches Your Travel Style Morocco Edition
seoTitle: What City Matches Your Travel Style Morocco Edition
description: Find out what city matches your travel style Morocco. Explore Fes for history, Marrakech for food, Essaouira for art, Chefchaouen for inspiration, Merzouga for desert adventure, and more.

blocks.x: What City Matches Your Travel Style Morocco? Every traveler dreams of a destination that reflects their personality, and Morocco is the perfect country to find that match. From the vibrant energy of Marrakech to the calm blue streets of Chefchaouen, each city offers a unique experience. Some places immerse you in history and culture, while others invite you to relax by the sea or seek adventure in the desert.
This guide will help you discover the Moroccan city that best fits your travel style—whether you’re a foodie, an adventurer, a history buff, or someone in search of beauty and inspiration.
For History & Culture Lovers → Fes

If you’re the type of traveler who can spend hours exploring ancient streets, tracing the footsteps of scholars and artisans, and marveling at centuries-old architecture, Fes is your ultimate Moroccan match.

As Morocco’s oldest imperial city and often called the country’s cultural and spiritual capital, Fes feels like stepping into a living museum. Its crown jewel is the medina of Fes el-Bali, a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of the largest car-free urban zones in the world. Inside its maze of more than 9,000 narrow alleys, you’ll encounter local life at its purest: merchants selling handwoven carpets, the aroma of fresh bread from communal ovens, and craftsmen shaping copperware just as their ancestors did.
Highlights for History Lovers
University of Al-Qarawiyyin – Founded in 859, it is recognized by UNESCO and Guinness World Records as the oldest continuously operating university in the world.
Bou Inania Madrasa – A masterpiece of Marinid architecture, with intricately carved cedarwood and colorful zellij tilework.
Chouara Tannery – A living tradition where leather has been dyed in stone vats for centuries; one of the city’s most photographed sites.
Mellah (Jewish Quarter) – A quieter part of the medina, with synagogues and a cemetery that reflect the city’s multicultural past.
The Fes Experience

Traveling in Fes isn’t about rushing from one attraction to another—it’s about immersion. Every turn reveals something unexpected: a hidden fountain, a historic caravanserai, or a family-run spice shop with recipes passed down for generations. History isn’t behind glass here; it’s alive in daily rituals, architecture, and crafts.
Unlike modern Casablanca or trendy Essaouira, Fes keeps its traditions close. Don’t be surprised if you feel transported back in time—that sense of preservation is part of the city’s magic.
Travel Style Match
Fes is the perfect destination if you are
A history buff who loves ancient cities, museums, and heritage tours.
A cultural explorer who enjoys connecting with local artisans and traditions.
A wanderer at heart who finds joy in getting lost in winding streets filled with stories from the past.
For Trendsetters & Modern Explorers → Casablanca

If your travel style leans toward the contemporary, with an eye for modern design, cosmopolitan culture, and vibrant nightlife, Casablanca is the city that will match your pace. Unlike Morocco’s historic imperial cities, Casablanca is forward-looking, blending traditional Moroccan identity with a sleek, international outlook.

This coastal hub is Morocco’s largest city and its economic capital. It may not have the labyrinthine charm of Fes or the souk-filled chaos of Marrakech, but it offers something unique: a chance to experience Morocco’s modern heartbeat. Here, stylish cafés, art galleries, and shopping centers sit alongside historic monuments and traditional markets, creating a fascinating contrast.
Highlights for Modern Explorers
Hassan II Mosque – One of the largest mosques in the world, rising dramatically over the Atlantic with its intricate Moroccan craftsmanship and towering minaret.
The Corniche – A lively seaside promenade lined with cafés, restaurants, and nightlife venues, perfect for enjoying the ocean breeze.
Art Deco Architecture – Casablanca’s downtown is filled with elegant 20th-century Art Deco buildings, a legacy of its colonial past.
The Morocco Mall – The largest shopping center in Africa, combining global brands with Moroccan design elements.
The Casablanca Experience

Casablanca is a city of balance. You can explore traditional markets like the Habous Quarter in the morning, admire the impressive Hassan II Mosque in the afternoon, and spend your evening dining in a rooftop restaurant overlooking the Atlantic. It’s ideal for travelers who want a mix of Moroccan culture without giving up the conveniences and rhythms of a modern metropolis.
Unlike more tourist-heavy cities, Casablanca also offers a glimpse into everyday Moroccan urban life. It’s not curated for visitors—it’s real, busy, and unapologetically modern.
Travel Style Match
Casablanca is the perfect destination if you are
A trendsetter who enjoys modern cities with a global feel.
A traveler who prefers cultural balance—mixing tradition with contemporary comforts.
Someone who values nightlife, dining, and shopping alongside sightseeing.
For Art & Seaside Lovers → Essaouira

If your ideal trip combines a laid-back coastal atmosphere with creative energy, Essaouira is the city that will capture your heart. Known as Morocco’s “Wind City of Africa,” it has long been a magnet for artists, musicians, and free spirits drawn to its relaxed pace and bohemian charm.

Essaouira’s walled medina, recognized as a UNESCO World Heritage Site , offers a calmer and more intimate experience than the bustling souks of Marrakech or Fes. Its whitewashed buildings with blue shutters, narrow lanes, and small artisan workshops create a sense of tranquility. The Atlantic breeze that sweeps through the streets gives the city a refreshing openness, making it a favorite escape for both locals and international visitors.
Highlights for Seaside Dreamers and Art Lovers
The Medina – Smaller and easier to navigate than Fes or Marrakech, perfect for browsing local crafts like thuya woodwork, textiles, and jewelry.
The Skala de la Ville – A historic sea bastion with cannons overlooking the Atlantic, once guarding the city against invaders.
Essaouira Beach – A wide, sandy stretch ideal for walks, camel rides, and watersports such as kitesurfing and windsurfing.
Gnaoua World Music Festival – An internationally renowned annual music event celebrating spiritual Gnaoua rhythms along with global sounds.
The Essaouira Experience

Essaouira is about slowing down and savoring life’s simple pleasures. You might spend your morning sipping mint tea in a seaside café, your afternoon exploring art galleries tucked into old riads, and your evening enjoying fresh seafood straight from the port. Unlike Marrakech’s intensity, Essaouira feels intimate and breezy, making it the perfect retreat for those who want culture without chaos.

It has also been a source of inspiration for countless creatives, from Jimi Hendrix in the 1960s to contemporary Moroccan artists. The city thrives on this energy, offering travelers not just relaxation but also a sense of creative renewal.
Travel Style Match
Essaouira is the perfect destination if you are
An art lover who enjoys galleries, music, and cultural festivals.
A seaside traveler who prefers calm beaches over crowded resorts.
Someone who appreciates a slower pace, charming architecture, and a bohemian vibe.
For Blue Dreamers & Soulful Wanderers → Chefchaouen

If your travel style is guided by beauty, tranquility, and a search for inspiration, then Chefchaouen—the famous “Blue Pearl” of Morocco—is your match. Nestled in the Rif Mountains of northern Morocco, this city is instantly recognizable for its serene blue-washed streets that feel more like an artist’s canvas than an ordinary town.

Unlike the busy urban centers of Casablanca or Marrakech, Chefchaouen offers calm and intimacy. The blue tones that coat walls, doors, and staircases create a dreamlike atmosphere, making it a favorite destination for photographers, couples, and anyone seeking a reflective escape.
Highlights for Soulful Wanderers
The Medina – A compact, relaxed maze of blue alleyways, artisan shops, and welcoming cafés, perfect for unhurried exploration.
The Kasbah Museum – Located in the heart of the medina, it houses ethnographic exhibits and offers peaceful gardens and views from its towers.
Spanish Mosque Viewpoint – A short hike outside the city that rewards you with breathtaking panoramic views, especially at sunset.
Local Handicrafts – Known for wool garments, woven blankets, and traditional crafts that reflect the mountain culture.
The Chefchaouen Experience

Life in Chefchaouen unfolds slowly. It is a place where you can spend your mornings wandering through quiet streets, your afternoons hiking into the Rif Mountains, and your evenings enjoying tagine in a cozy terrace restaurant. The pace encourages you to disconnect from the rush of everyday life and reconnect with yourself.

What sets Chefchaouen apart is its atmosphere. The blue walls are not just beautiful; they create a sense of peace and harmony, which is why so many visitors describe the city as meditative and even spiritual. For those seeking inspiration—whether through photography, writing, or simply reflection—Chefchaouen offers the perfect canvas.
Travel Style Match
Chefchaouen is the perfect destination if you are
A dreamer who finds joy in beauty, color, and atmosphere.
A romantic or photographer searching for inspiring landscapes.
A traveler who prefers slower-paced exploration and quiet mountain surroundings.
Discover Your Moroccan Match

Ready to explore the city that aligns with your travel style? Start planning your Moroccan adventure today and experience the culture, landscapes, and flavors that will resonate most with you. Every city offers its own story—find the one that speaks to yours.
Click Here
For Desert Adventurers → Merzouga

If your idea of travel is chasing once-in-a-lifetime experiences and immersing yourself in nature’s raw beauty, then Merzouga—gateway to the Sahara Desert—will match your adventurous spirit. Located near the Algerian border, this small village sits on the edge of the vast Erg Chebbi dunes , where golden sand stretches endlessly toward the horizon.

Unlike Morocco’s cities with bustling medinas, Merzouga offers a completely different rhythm of life. Here, time slows down, and the desert itself becomes the attraction. From camel treks at sunset to nights under star-filled skies, Merzouga offers the kind of transformative journey many travelers place at the top of their bucket list.
Highlights for Adventure Seekers
Camel Trekking – The quintessential Sahara experience, riding through rolling dunes as the sun sets over the desert.
Luxury or Nomadic Desert Camps – Spend the night in traditional Berber-style tents or opt for luxury camps with comfortable beds, gourmet meals, and cultural performances around the fire.
Sandboarding – For the thrill-seekers, the dunes make a natural playground for this desert sport.
Star Gazing – With no city lights, the Sahara sky offers some of the clearest views of the Milky Way you’ll ever see.
Day Trips to Khamlia Village – Famous for its Gnaoua music and warm hospitality, offering a cultural glimpse into desert life.
The Merzouga Experience

Merzouga is more than a destination—it’s an immersion. The desert teaches patience and simplicity. Mornings begin with breathtaking sunrises that paint the dunes in shades of gold and orange. Days are spent exploring the desert by 44, visiting nomadic families, or simply enjoying the silence that only the Sahara can provide. Nights end with traditional drumming under a canopy of stars.

The journey to Merzouga itself is part of the adventure, often taken through the High Atlas Mountains, lush valleys, and traditional kasbah villages, making it a true road trip experience before even reaching the desert.
Travel Style Match
Merzouga is the perfect destination if you are
An adventurer seeking iconic, once-in-a-lifetime experiences.
A nature lover who values landscapes and quiet over urban bustle.
A bucket-list traveler dreaming of camel treks, starry skies, and desert camps.
For Politics & Culture Enthusiasts → Rabat

If you enjoy cities that balance history with modern life, and you appreciate places that are organized, clean, and less chaotic, Rabat may be the Moroccan city that matches your travel style. As the political capital of Morocco, Rabat combines its role as a government hub with cultural heritage, historic monuments, and a calmer atmosphere compared to Marrakech or Fes.

Rabat often surprises visitors. While it might not have the instant name recognition of Marrakech, it offers wide boulevards, palm-lined avenues, and a coastline along the Atlantic. It is modern and administrative, yet also steeped in history, with ancient kasbahs, medinas, and ruins woven into its urban fabric.
Highlights for Balanced Travelers
Kasbah of the Udayas – A picturesque 12th-century fortress overlooking the Bou Regreg River, with Andalusian gardens and ocean views.

Hassan Tower and Mausoleum of Mohammed V – An unfinished mosque from the 12th century paired with the stunning mausoleum of Morocco’s modern kings, symbolizing the country’s continuity between past and present.
Rabat Medina – Less crowded than Marrakech or Fes, making it ideal for shopping without stress.
Chellah Necropolis – Ancient Roman and Islamic ruins surrounded by gardens and storks’ nests, offering a peaceful yet historic escape.
The Mohammed VI Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art – A modern institution showcasing Moroccan and international art.
The Rabat Experience

Life in Rabat feels balanced. In one day, you can admire ancient ruins at Chellah, stroll through modern museums, and then relax on the city’s sandy beaches. The city also reflects Morocco’s political heartbeat, with embassies, ministries, and diplomatic neighborhoods shaping its identity.

For travelers who want Morocco’s culture but prefer less noise and intensity, Rabat offers an approachable and elegant experience. It’s an excellent destination for those who enjoy structure, history, and modern comfort blended seamlessly together.
Travel Style Match
Rabat is the perfect destination if you are
A traveler who values culture without chaos.
Someone who enjoys a mix of historic sites and modern attractions.
Interested in Morocco’s political and administrative role alongside its heritage.
For Foodies & Shoppers → Marrakech

If your travel style revolves around vibrant energy, bold colors, and rich flavors, Marrakech is your Moroccan match. Known as the “Red City” for its terracotta buildings, Marrakech is a sensory feast: bustling souks, aromatic spices, street performers, and ornate palaces create an unforgettable experience for travelers who thrive in lively environments.

Marrakech is perfect for those who love to dive into local life. Every corner of the city offers something new, whether it’s a hidden café tucked into a riad, a spice vendor in the medina, or a street musician performing in Djemaa el-Fna. Here, Moroccan culture is intense, immediate, and irresistible.
Highlights for Foodies and Shoppers
Djemaa el-Fna – The central square transforms from a market by day into a hub of food stalls, storytellers, and musicians by night.
The Souks – A labyrinth of markets selling spices, textiles, jewelry, leather goods, and traditional crafts. Each souk has its specialty, making every turn a new adventure.
Bahia Palace – A stunning example of Moroccan architecture, with ornate gardens, carved ceilings, and intricate tilework.

Jardin Majorelle & Yves Saint Laurent Museum – A peaceful garden oasis filled with exotic plants and the vibrant colors of artist Jacques Majorelle, complemented by the fashion exhibits of Yves Saint Laurent.
Traditional Moroccan Cuisine – Sample tagine, couscous, pastilla, and street foods like msemen and harira in a variety of local restaurants.
The Marrakech Experience

Visiting Marrakech is about embracing energy and variety. Spend your mornings wandering the souks, your afternoons exploring palaces and gardens, and your evenings dining under lantern light while listening to local musicians. Marrakech can be intense, but it rewards those who immerse themselves fully.
It’s also a city that caters to both adventure and luxury. From traditional riads to modern boutique hotels, visitors can choose how they want to experience Morocco’s most famous city.
Travel Style Match
Marrakech is the perfect destination if you are
A foodie who loves tasting local flavors at markets and restaurants.
A shopper seeking unique handcrafted souvenirs and vibrant bazaars.
A traveler energized by lively streets, culture, and bold, colorful experiences.
Conclusion

Morocco is a country of contrasts, where each city offers a distinct personality and experience. From the ancient alleys of Fes to the modern energy of Casablanca, the seaside charm of Essaouira, the serene blue streets of Chefchaouen, the golden dunes of Merzouga, the balanced elegance of Rabat, and the vibrant chaos of Marrakech, there is a Moroccan city for every type of traveler.

No matter your travel style—whether you seek history, adventure, relaxation, art, or culinary delights—Morocco provides a perfect match. By understanding your own preferences and what excites you most about travel, you can select the city that will make your Moroccan journey unforgettable.
